newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Chretien stays fiscal course in shuffle.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Chretien stays fiscal course in shuffle.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien, whose Liberal government was re-elected last week with a reduced majority, shuffled his cabinet on Wednesday but maintained his highly regarded economic team.

Chretien reappointed the tight-fisted Paul Martin as finance minister. Martin won international praise for slashing the Canadian budget deficit in the Liberals' first term and his reappointment had been eagerly sought by financial markets.
"The economic team is totally unchanged," Chretien spokesman Peter Donolo told Reuters.
"I think it's a very strong message about direction, about continuity, about seeing through the (deficit reduction) plan," Donolo said.
Donolo spoke moments before the cabinet was sworn in at Rideau Hall, official residence of the Canadian representative of Britain's Queen Elizabeth, who is Canada's head of state.
Chretien said in a statement that the job of the new cabinet was "to complete the task of balancing the budget and putting Canada's finances on a sound and sustainable footing."

But in a possible signal the goverment would increase spending on social programmes, he added that it would seek to modernise and expand Canada's government-run health care system and "provide for the well-being of our children."

Chretien relieved left-leaning Heritage Minister Sheila Copps of her additional role as deputy prime minister. Former government house leader Herb Gray succeeded Copps in the deputy prime minister's post.
In the aftermath of the June 2 election, in which the Liberals lost heavily in economically depressed Atlantic Canada, some Liberal legislators urged the party to veer to the left in a second term.
But Chretien reappointed John Manley -- viewed, like Martin, as a fiscal conservative -- as industry minister.
Justice Minister Allan Rock was moved to the health portfolio, a job that Copps had reportedly sought amid improving prospects for a budget surplus in coming years.

Environment Minister Sergio Marchi became international trade minister, replacing Art Eggleton, who moved to the sensitive defence portfolio, succeeding the acerbic Doug Young, who was defeated in the election.
Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy, seen as an advocate of human rights in a government whose foreign policy has focused more on promoting Canadian exports, stayed in his post.
The Chretien government shifted its focus on justice and social issues by appointing as justice minister Anne McLellan, who narrowly won re-election in the conservative western province of Alberta.

Her predecessor, Rock, angered conservative groups by tightening gun control and expanding rights for homosexuals. The Reform Party, which won most of the seats in Western Canada, campaigned on a tough and order policy. Most of its members are also conservative on social issues.
The new cabinet was expanded by two members to 36, including Chretien and junior ministers.
In the election, the Liberals won 155 of the 301 seats in the House of Commons. Reform ousted the separatist Bloc Quebecois as the official opposition, winning 60 seats to the Bloc's 44.
